So, I just finished Fantastic Four and FF. Here's a brief summary of the key points relevant going forward:

  • The Infinity Gauntlet only works in its native universe.

  • Black Bolt is the celestial messiah of the Inhumans, whose city is currently above Manhattan.

  • The Kree and Inhumans now have a shared destiny "Until everything dies." They will work in opposition to that.

  • "After the last war when all reality has collapsed into a single timestream and the heat death of everything is imminent, there is a white space where your son (Franklin Richards) sits waiting for the new future we have created to overtake him. There, post-collapse, he acts as an anchor for the changes he made."

  • Reed and T'Challa's fates are bound together; the Panther god tells him that the events of AvX are nothing compared to what follows.

  • AIM sets up a nation in the Caribbean.

  • Doom's time as god of his own dimensionand subsequent overthrow possibly signals a major character change.

Such a great memory. I was young, but fascinated by the idea of a computer. Back then. computers were these big, abstract things. You would never get to touch one, but you could watch them work behind glass. When I was about six or so, my neighbor asked me if I would like to see a computer in his house. My Mom and I went over, and I imagined this giant machine, filling his basement.

Instead it was a box. It was blue (?) and had a series of switches and lights on it. He had built it himself out of a kit. It was called the Altair, and it was the first personal computer. No monitor. No keyboard. You entered the program, by hand, with the switches in front, and the output was through the lights.

It didn't matter that this computer didn't "do" anything I could appreciate. The fact that he had his own computer was the cool part.

A few years later he would get an Apple II, and I would discover the joy of playing computer games at home.

I would later get a newspaper route to buy my own computer.

I think perhaps my very first original memory was with Donkey Kong handhelds, technically that is a computer. This later extended to an Atari. And from there Arcade machines, then on to ZX Spectrum, Spectra Video and Commodore 64.

TRS-80

I used some sort of database program to enter all my dad's records into a database. I was so super proud I could tell him he had 1018 records, 64 from Chrysalis, 9 Todd Rundgren, 11 Elton John...

That was a summer well spent.
My earliest computer memory was 64mb which was fast at the time
Windows 3.1, Math Blaster and Reader Rabbit on a 386 with 8 MB of RAM
Trying to figure out how my dad's MS-DOS PC worked and deleting all of his tax information...but then I got to play battle chess!

Late 1980's. I was a just a little guy at the time, and I had to stay in the back room at my grandparent's business sometimes while my mom was at work. They had a giant and noisy dot matrix printer that got my attention more than the actual computer. The sound was like nothing I had ever heard, and I was a bit mesmerized watching the print head travel back and forth while words appeared under it. I must have been quite young because I remember learning to tie my shoes there too. The first time I actually got to use a computer was 2nd grade. They let us play Oregon trail, Wheel of Fortune, and some purely educational stuff. Around this time, my dad bought me a Game Boy, and I have had a life-long fascination with computer software and hardware.

The sound of my dads dot matrix printer, them things made a racket.

The Floppy disc games on MS-Dos:

  • Prince of Persia

  • One where you would shoot down planes that flew across the top of the screen before the men parachuted out. If they parachuted you would have to shoot them too, because if enough got to the ground they would build a tower of men and grenade your turret. Anyone know the name of this game?
Obsessively playing Red Alert 2 on my dad's computer.
Some Tandy my father found in a dumpster. Worked on it, never looked back. Can barely remember it as most of childhood is either blank or a blurr.
Playing the original Duke Nukem (side scroller) on DOS.
My earliest is a little fuzzy but I remember having to go through some program and answer questions on a white box machine for school. This was in very early grade school.
DOS and a telnet type game where you navigate a dungeon and try to rescue a princess. I was around 4-5 so I can't remember the details.

My earliest memory is age 4.

I asked mother if I could be excused after dinner. She said yes, so I climbed out of my chair (which was as tall as me) waddled over to the office, booted up the computer, and popped in the pajama Sam disk.
I remember playing educational games on an Apple III in kindergarten. The best part was switching the floppy disk for a new game.
I remember in 1974, playing around in the computer "room" at Mankato State. teletype and keyboard .
In '93 or so, I remember accidentally deleting one of my mom's college papers... oops.
I remember around early 1999, where Windows 95 was around and literally was the only alternative to Mac - as Linux hadn't even left Usenet at the time.

Two things. The sound of dial up as your computer connected and seeing my first horse on girl pic. Stay with me on this. Back in the day pictures loaded line by line and at first I could tell it was a horse but what the heck else was going... OMG! I have never clicked the back button so many times in my life. I turned off the computer for three days and waited for the police to show up.
Dungeon Keeper, baby. Played the shit out of it, that game was amazing.

I remember learning how to type on an Apple IIc back in 2nd grade and I also remember going to computer lab to play math games. I've been hacking and working on computers ever since, it's one of the few things I've actually stuck with throughout my life.

We also had a Commodore PET in my 4th glad class that we used to play The Weather Game once in a while. Waiting for the cassettes to load was like an eternity. :D

I've had a computer in my home for my entire life. I'm sure there was something prior to this, but the first memory that pops up was playing through Castle Adventure.

I remember watching lots of progress bars too. When a hard drive was being reformatted or defragmented or an especially long install was going, I'd still just sit there and listen to all the noises.

A few years later, I found a book in the public library titled something to the effect of "How To Make Your Own Computer Games", learned BASIC, and made some simple games. After my parents saw that I had the interest, they bought me a textbook on VB6.

After typing this, I started to think I missed those days, then remembered how ridiculously slow, expensive, clunky and loud the machines were and how terrible most of the software was.
